_readme: Who each company is, for the Introduction tab: a short blurb, the parent's own site in China
(or global) and its US site where one exists, and a slot for a representative photo of one of
its outlets in China. LINKS ARE PROVIDED AS-IS. Any link outside the USA is untested by this
project and should be treated at the reader's discretion — the site warns of this beside every
such link. PHOTOS are not shipped: `photo` names a local file under map/img/ that must be an
image the project has the right to use (licensed, or an official press image with permission);
until one is added the tab shows a neutral placeholder. Never hotlink a copyrighted storefront
photo. `photo_credit` is shown beneath the image when present.

mixue.name: MIXUE
mixue.blurb: The world's largest fast-food chain by store count, with nearly 60,000 outlets. It runs on very low prices, such as an ice cream cone for under a dollar, and a franchise model that makes most of its money selling ingredients to franchisees. Its mascot is a crowned Snow King. US stores began opening in 2025.

chagee.name: CHAGEE
chagee.blurb: A fast-growing premium tea brand whose Chinese name is Bawang Chaji. It is often described as China's answer to Starbucks, and is known for its oolong-milk teas and plain branding. It listed on Nasdaq in 2025 and opened its first US stores the same year.

luckin.name: Luckin Coffee
luckin.blurb: China's largest coffee chain. It passed Starbucks in China by volume, using cheap, app-first ordering, and did so after rebuilding from a 2020 accounting fraud that had it delisted. It opened its first US stores in New York in mid-2025.

miniso.name: MINISO
miniso.blurb: A variety retailer selling cheap, design-focused goods and licensed-character merchandise, with a Japanese-styled look despite its Guangzhou roots. It has the largest and most established US presence of any chain tracked here.

popmart.name: POP MART
popmart.blurb: The blind-box toy company behind Labubu and other collectible figures, sold through staffed stores and unstaffed “Robo Shop” vending kiosks. Its US presence has grown quickly in malls across the country.
popmart.first_outlet: East Rutherford, NJ — American Dream (first permanent store)

haidilao.name: Haidilao
haidilao.blurb: A large hot pot chain known for its elaborate service, which can include free manicures, live noodle-pulling and birthday songs. Its overseas arm, Super Hi International, runs the US restaurants, and it has been in the US since 2013.
haidilao.first_outlet: Arcadia, CA — 400 S Baldwin Ave (Westfield Santa Anita)

heytea.name: HEYTEA
heytea.blurb: The brand that made cheese-foam and fresh-fruit tea popular in China, at the premium end of the market. Its US stores cluster in Chinese-American neighbourhoods. It publishes no US store locator, so we put its footprint together from public records.

cotti.name: Cotti Coffee
cotti.blurb: Founded in 2022 by two executives who had been forced out of Luckin, and set up in direct competition with it. Cotti competes on price and has expanded worldwide very fast on a franchise model. Its US growth is quiet and led by franchisees, with no public US locator.
cotti.first_outlet: Pearl City, HI — Pearl Highlands Center

taier.name: Tai Er
taier.blurb: A Sichuan sauerkraut-fish (suancai yu) restaurant from the Hong Kong-listed group Jiumaojiu, known for its stylised branding and one signature dish. Its US presence is small and new, in San Mateo, San Jose, Flushing and LA.
taier.first_outlet: City of Industry, CA — 18518 E Gale Ave

chabaidao.name: ChaPanda
chabaidao.blurb: A large Chinese fruit-tea chain (Chabaidao) that listed in Hong Kong in 2024. It entered the US in 2025 trading as “TeaByDo”, with only a handful of stores so far.

nayuki.name: NaiSnow
nayuki.blurb: The US arm of Nayuki (Naixue), a premium Hong Kong-listed tea-and-soft-bread chain, trading in America as “NaiSnow”. It entered the US in late 2025 and is expanding quickly across New York and into New Jersey.

juewei.name: Juewei
juewei.blurb: A Shanghai-listed braised-snack chain (“duck neck” and other marinated items) with tens of thousands of outlets in China. Its US presence is tiny and mostly delivery, trading as Juewei Yabo, Jue Wei Kitchen and Jue Wei Food.

yangguofu.name: Yangguofu
yangguofu.blurb: One of China's two dominant malatang (build-your-own skewered hotpot soup) chains, founded in Harbin in 2003. It began a registered US franchise programme in 2024, trading as YGF, and is expanding across the coasts.

fishwithyou.name: Fish With You
fishwithyou.blurb: A Chinese fast-casual chain built on one dish: Sichuan sauerkraut fish (suancai yu) over rice. Founded in Beijing around 2016, it has thousands of outlets in China. In the US it trades under several names (Fish With You, YONNY, Wei's Fish), using per-store sites rather than one locator.

yangs.name: Yang's Braised Chicken Rice
yangs.blurb: A braised-chicken-over-rice brand that was one of the earliest Chinese chains in America, trading since 2017, but is now in retreat, with most of its US restaurants closed. We include it because it is here, and because tracking a chain that opens and then quietly closes is part of the point of a daily count.

zhangliang.name: Zhang Liang Malatang
zhangliang.blurb: One of China's two dominant malatang (build-your-own skewered hotpot soup) chains, alongside Yangguofu, founded in Harbin in 2008 with around 6,000 outlets. Its self-serve format lets diners fill a bowl from 80-plus fresh ingredients cooked in a spicy bone broth. Its own brand news reports 42 North American outlets across the US, Canada and Mexico as of September 2026; in the US it clusters in California, in the Bay Area and Los Angeles.

chahalo.name: ChaHalo
chahalo.blurb: A premium "modern Chinese tea" chain founded in 2016 in Xi'an, known for tea-forward drinks made with whole tea leaves and fresh milk and a signature "tri-aroma" style. It has grown to around 1,000 stores across China and began expanding overseas in 2024; its early US outlets are in California and New York, with Canada (Toronto) also underway.

xiaolongkan.name: Shoo Loong Kan Hotpot
xiaolongkan.blurb: A Sichuan (mala) hotpot chain founded in Chengdu in 2014, one of China's largest with thousands of outlets, known for its numbing-spicy broth and old-Chengdu styling. It trades in the US as "Shoo Loong Kan Hotpot" and — unusually for the chains here — publishes its own US store locator.

liuyishou.name: Liuyishou Hot Pot
liuyishou.blurb: A Chongqing hotpot chain founded in 2000, one of China's largest with thousands of outlets, known for its buttery mala broth and beef. It trades across North America as "Liuyishou Hot Pot" and publishes its own site with a page per city; its US outlets run from Boston and New York to California, Texas, Illinois and Washington.

aunteajenny.name: Auntea Jenny
aunteajenny.blurb: A bubble-tea chain founded in 2013 in Shanghai, one of China's largest with several thousand outlets and a 2025 Hong Kong listing, known for fresh-brewed milk teas and grain-based drinks. It entered the US as "Auntea Jenny", with its first outlets in New York and California and many more announced.

mollytea.name: Molly Tea
mollytea.blurb: A Chinese premium milk-tea chain founded in 2021, known for its jasmine-tea "milk white" drinks and fast overseas growth across Asia, Australia and North America. Its US outlets, trading as "Molly Tea", run across California and into Washington, Texas, Illinois, Georgia, Nevada, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and beyond.
mollytea.first_outlet: Flushing, Queens, NY — 37-11 Prince St (since closed)

lelecha.name: Lelecha
lelecha.blurb: A premium "modern Chinese tea" chain founded in 2016 in Shanghai, known for cheese-foam teas, fruit teas and its dirty-bun bakery. It has begun opening in the US, though its US site is not yet public; early outlets are in California.

nonggengji.name: Nong Geng Ji
nonggengji.blurb: A Hunan-cuisine restaurant chain from Shenzhen known for countryside-style, wok-charred cooking with fresh peppers and family-style dishes. Its first US restaurant opened in Flushing, Queens in January 2026, with a second announced for Rockville, Maryland.

baospastry.name: Bao's Pastry
baospastry.blurb: A Beijing-headquartered bakery chain founded by Bao Caisheng about two decades ago, famous in China for its pork-floss cakes and cream-filled sponge, with more than 100 outlets. Its first US store opened in Flushing, Queens in late 2025.

toptoy.name: TOP TOY
toptoy.blurb: A Chinese art-toy and blind-box retailer launched in 2020 by MINISO Group, carrying its own IPs alongside licensed lines from Sanrio, Disney and others. It opened its first US store in Times Square, New York.

toys52.name: 52Toys
toys52.blurb: A Chinese designer-toy and blind-box brand founded in 2015 in Beijing, known for its Panda Roll and BEASTBOX lines and mecha model kits. Its US retail presence has begun in Georgia, alongside an online store.

dezhuang.name: De Zhuang Hot Pot
dezhuang.blurb: A Chongqing hot-pot restaurant and seasoning group founded in 1999 by Li Dejian, grown to some 900 restaurants across China. Known for numbing-spicy Chongqing broth. It reached the US around early 2025 with a full hot-pot restaurant in Manhattan's East Village and a smaller 'De Hotpot Mini' express store near Seattle.
dezhuang.first_outlet: New York — 37 St Marks Pl (East Village)

meizhoudongpo.name: Meizhou Dongpo
meizhoudongpo.blurb: A Sichuan-cuisine sit-down chain founded in Beijing in 1996 by Wang Gang and Liang Di and named for the poet Su Dongpo. With about 114 restaurants in China, it was one of the earliest Chinese chains to reach America, opening a Los Angeles flagship in 2013. Two California restaurants remain open after several LA-area closures.
meizhoudongpo.first_outlet: Los Angeles — 10250 Santa Monica Blvd (Century City)

shudaxia.name: Shu Da Xia Hotpot
shudaxia.blurb: A Chengdu hot-pot chain founded in 2015, styled around wuxia (martial-arts) imagery, with 600-plus outlets. Since 2023 it has been owned by the Xiaolongkan hot-pot group. Its single US restaurant, near Boston University, has operated since May 2022.

xibei.name: Xibei
xibei.blurb: The flagship brand of the Xibei group, which grew from a 1988 snack shop in Inner Mongolia into some 370 restaurants serving Northwestern-China oat-noodle and mutton dishes. Its US expansion began in Los Angeles in December 2024 and now spans four Southern California outlets under three names — a flagship, a dumpling shop and fast-casual 'Eatery' noodle bars.
xibei.first_outlet: Los Angeles — 3300 W Sunset Blvd (Silver Lake)

grandmashome.name: Grandma's Home
grandmashome.blurb: A Hangzhou-cuisine chain founded in 1998 by Wu Guoping, known for affordable home-style Jiangnan cooking across 200-plus directly-run restaurants in China. Its first and so far only US restaurant opened in Manhattan's Flatiron district in early 2024.

xijiade.name: Dumpling Xi
xijiade.blurb: A Northeastern-China shrimp-dumpling chain founded in 2002 in Hegang, Heilongjiang by Gao Defu, with 800-plus directly-operated stores. It trades in America as 'Dumpling Xi', opening its first US store in Flushing, Queens in February 2025 and a second in the East Village that July.

malubianbian.name: Ma Lu Bian Bian
malubianbian.blurb: A Chengdu chain founded in 2015 in the 'chuan chuan' style — DIY skewers cooked in a shared spicy hot pot — done up like a nostalgic 1980s roadside stall. It claims over a thousand outlets globally. Its US footprint has churned heavily since the first store opened in San Gabriel in 2019; an Orlando restaurant is the clearest currently-open location.
malubianbian.first_outlet: San Gabriel, CA — 301 W Valley Blvd (now closed)

feidachu.name: Chef Fei
feidachu.blurb: A Hunan-cuisine chain built on one signature dish — stir-fried pork with chili peppers (辣椒炒肉) — founded by Fei Lianghui in Hengyang, Hunan and unified under the 费大厨 name in 2016, with roughly 200 directly-managed restaurants across China. Marketed in America as 'China's King of Stir-Fry', it opened its first US restaurant at Westfield UTC in San Diego in September 2026.
feidachu.first_outlet: San Diego — 4301 La Jolla Village Dr (Westfield UTC)

dalongyi.name: Da Long Yi Hot Pot
dalongyi.blurb: A Chengdu hot-pot chain founded in 2013 in the city's Yulin district, grown through franchising to a claimed 2,000-plus stores with outlets abroad. Known for numbing-spicy Sichuan broth. Its US outlets run as independent franchises; two — in Long Island City and Boston — are currently open after earlier California and Seattle stores closed.
dalongyi.first_outlet: San Gabriel, CA — 250 W Valley Blvd (now closed)

shuyi.name: Shuyi Grass Jelly & Tea
shuyi.blurb: A grass-jelly milk-tea chain founded in 2007 in Chengdu by Wang Bin, whose signature drinks pile a cup half-full with grass jelly and other toppings; one of China's largest tea chains, with several thousand stores. Its US shops, trading as 'Shuyi Grass Jelly & Tea', are franchise-run — three are open in Virginia and the Bay Area after the original San Mateo store closed.
shuyi.first_outlet: San Mateo, CA — 165 E 4th Ave (now closed)

anta.name: Anta
anta.blurb: China's largest sportswear company, founded in 1991 in Jinjiang, Fujian, and listed in Hong Kong. The Anta brand runs roughly 9,900 stores across Greater China; its parent group also owns or controls FILA, Descente and Amer Sports (Arc'teryx, Salomon, Wilson), though those are not Chinese brands and are tracked separately. Anta opened its first US store — a company-operated flagship in Beverly Hills — in February 2026, with NBA players it sponsors at the launch, and is expanding across Southeast Asia.
anta.first_outlet: Beverly Hills, CA — 330 N Beverly Dr

urbanrevivo.name: Urban Revivo
urbanrevivo.blurb: A Guangzhou fashion retailer founded in 2006 and often called China's answer to Zara, known for large, design-led stores. It runs more than 400 stores, mostly in China and Southeast Asia, and has since expanded to the UK and the US; its parent, Fashion Momentum Group, is privately held. Urban Revivo opened its first US store — a roughly 30,000-square-foot flagship in SoHo — in February 2025.

jnby.name: JNBY
jnby.blurb: A Hangzhou designer-fashion house, listed in Hong Kong, that runs a family of in-house women's and lifestyle labels — JNBY, Croquis, less, jnby by JNBY and Pomme de terre — across roughly 2,100 stores, almost all in China. In the United States its stores trade as “AGoodFun”, run by a local licensee, with locations in San Francisco and Seattle; earlier stores in Bellevue and SoHo, New York have closed.
jnby.first_outlet: Seattle, WA — 600 Pine St (Pacific Place), as AGoodFun
